abstract_sentences.text: Reasoning models often spend a significant amount of time thinking before they generate a visible response.

evidence.anchor: spend a significant amount of time thinking before ... visible response

abstract_sentences.text: In the meantime, they do not give the user any hints as to whether their reasoning is on the right track, and do not give the user any recourse to stop and correct them if their reasoning is flawed.

evidence.anchor: no hints ... no recourse to stop and correct

abstract_sentences.text: This creates a frustrating, but unfortunately common, experience: the user’s time is wasted while the model reasons from a false premise that could have easily been corrected.

evidence.anchor: user’s time is wasted ... false premise

abstract_sentences.text: In contrast, human speakers typically perform lightweight, incremental grounding acts to ensure that participants in the conversation are on the same page; here we ask if language models can learn to leverage a similar type of behavior?

evidence.anchor: lightweight, incremental grounding acts

abstract_sentences.text: With this motivation, we propose interleaved reasoning (IR), in which the model alternates between thinking and surfacing intermediate responses, as an alternative to the standard “think-then-answer” approach.

evidence.anchor: alternates between thinking and surfacing intermediate responses

abstract_sentences.text: By providing useful information to the user earlier, IR reduces perceived latency, the time a user waits for an initial output, without compromising the quality of the final response.

evidence.anchor: reduces perceived latency ... without compromising

abstract_sentences.text: We further introduce a specialization of interleaved reasoning, Plantain (Plan-Thought-Answer Interleaving), where the first intermediate response is an explicit, step-by-step plan for executing the task.

evidence.anchor: first intermediate response is an explicit, step-by-step plan

abstract_sentences.text: This plan-first strategy allows for user intervention and early feedback for subsequent reasoning steps.

evidence.anchor: user intervention and early feedback

abstract_sentences.text: We demonstrate that Plantain yields an ∼6% improvement in pass@1 across several challenging math reasoning and coding benchmarks, while reducing time-to-first-response by over 60% relative to think-then-answer baselines.

evidence.anchor: ∼6% improvement in pass@1 ... over 60%

final_judgment.single_storyline: Expose a short actionable plan before long reasoning, train that interleaving into the model, and use plan-level selection/rejection to prune bad paths before full rollout; the intended payoff is lower perceived latency with equal or higher pass@1.
final_judgment.main_body_keeps: Motivation, P→T→A contrast, interleaved trace notation, three-stage training, plan judge, Best-of-N/R&R algorithms, Q1/Q2, model/task/metric setup, Tables 1–4, and structured/verifiable scope.
final_judgment.appendix_moves: Full pseudocode, SI and autorater prompts, dataset sizes/descriptions, H100 and hyperparameters, synthetic trace controls, prompt/code examples, cross-domain plans, and TA/R&R qualitative traces move to A.1–A.10.
final_judgment.best_pattern: Figure 1 fixes the intervention unit; Table 2 compares plan-level against answer-level feedback; Table 3 tests budget scaling; Table 4 diagnoses rewind depth. The same short-plan unit links mechanism to evidence.
final_judgment.largest_gap: The coding-only generalization premise conflicts with the stated MATH500 training set, and p.9 mixes Table 1 and Table 3 values. Independently, human judgment, wall-clock/T/P cost, variance, and some denominators are missing.
final_judgment.transfer_rule: For interactive reasoning, make the first visible unit user-readable, conditionable by the model, and externally judgeable, then compare plan-level rejection with answer-level restart under matched tasks and budgets.
final_judgment.transfer_boundary: This transfers to structured tasks with verifiable plan signals and short intent-bearing prefixes; evidence remains open for ambiguous prompts, subjective preferences, judge-dominated latency, and real human responsiveness.
